draft.title: Separation of powers
card: The Constitution divides government power into three kinds, each given to a different body.
Legislative
the power to make laws. It is held by parliament.
Executive
the power to carry out laws and run government. It is held by the Governor-General, ministers and government departments.
Judicial
the power to decide disputes and apply the law. It is held by courts.
draft.remember: Three kinds of power are held by three different bodies, so no one body has too much.

a.q: Why does the Constitution give law-making, running government and deciding disputes to different bodies?
opts: So that no one body holds too much power
So that laws can be passed more quickly
So that courts can make laws when needed
So that ministers can decide disputes
a.why: Dividing the powers spreads them out, so no one body can control all of them. Speed is not the aim, and courts do not make laws.
a.clue: Think about what goes wrong if one body holds all power.

b.q: A federal court in Perth hears a dispute and decides which side is right under the law. Which kind of power is the court using?
opts: Judicial power
Legislative power
Executive power
Parliamentary power
b.why: Deciding disputes and applying the law is judicial power, which courts hold. Legislative power is making laws, and executive power is carrying them out.

a.best: So that no one body holds too much power

problems.detail: Why (a) says 'courts do not make laws'. VCE Units 3 and 4 teach that courts make law through precedent and statutory interpretation, so this is false in this course. It could say instead that the aim is not to let courts take over parliament's law-making role.

The card and the remember line say each power is given to 'a different body' or 'three different bodies'. In Australia the legislative and executive powers are not strictly separated: ministers must sit in parliament under responsible government, and only judicial power is strictly separate. The VCE study design expects students to know this, so the card gives a misleadingly strict picture.

The question names a court, and the clue asks which power belongs to courts. A Year 12 student can match 'court' to 'judicial' without understanding the idea, so the question is too easy for the level.

check.summary: The card presents all three powers as fully separate, but in Australia only judicial power is strictly separated: legislative and executive power overlap through responsible government. Why (a) wrongly says courts do not make laws, and question b is too easy for Year 12.

proposal.title: Separation of powers
card: The Constitution sets up three kinds of government power. Spreading them out means no one body holds too much power.
Legislative
the power to make laws. It is held by parliament.
Executive

the power to carry out laws and run government, used by the Governor-General, ministers and departments. Under responsible government, ministers must also sit in parliament and answer to it, so this power overlaps with legislative power.
Judicial
the power to decide disputes and apply the law. It is held only by courts, which are kept strictly separate from parliament and the executive.
proposal.remember: Power is spread so no one body has too much. Only judicial power is kept strictly apart.

a.q: Which statement about the separation of powers in Australia is correct?
opts: Judicial power is kept strictly separate from the others
All three powers are kept strictly separate from each other
Ministers are not allowed to be members of parliament
Courts share judicial power with ministers and parliament
a.why: Only courts hold judicial power, and they are kept strictly apart from the other two. All three are not strictly separate, because ministers sit in parliament, so legislative and executive power overlap.

b.q: Sam is a federal minister and a member of parliament. He votes for a bill, and once it is law his department carries it out. A friend says this breaks the separation of powers. Is the friend right?
opts: No, legislative and executive power overlap in Australia
Yes, each power must be held by a completely separate body
Yes, ministers are not meant to vote on their own bills
No, because ministers also hold some judicial power
b.why: Under responsible government, ministers sit in parliament, so legislative and executive power overlap. The friend assumes all three powers are strictly separate, but in Australia only judicial power is. Ministers do not hold judicial power, which belongs only to courts.
b.clue: Which two powers are not strictly kept apart?

a.best: Judicial power is kept strictly separate from the others

b.best: No, legislative and executive power overlap in Australia
